id_scheme: DOMAIN-NN. Identifiers are stable: a competency keeps its id even if its title is refined.

field_notes.outcomes: Observable abilities. Each begins with a verb that can be demonstrated and assessed, not with 'understand'.
field_notes.prerequisites: Edges carry the reason for the dependency, because a prerequisite graph without justification is decoration.
field_notes.source_coverage.status: sourced | partial | none. 'sourced' means the supplied book teaches the competency at the target level; 'partial' means it contributes but does not complete it; 'none' means no supplied source covers it yet.
field_notes.source_coverage.mml_sections: Section identifiers from knowledge/sources/mml/structure.json, verified against the source index.
field_notes.roadmap_skills: SK identifiers from the user's roadmaps (knowledge/roadmaps/consolidated-inventory.json).

competencies.name: Vectors, vector spaces and linear independence
competencies.why: Every model parameter, activation and embedding is a vector in a space whose structure determines what operations are legal.
outcomes: Decide whether a given set of vectors is linearly independent and justify the conclusion with a computation.
Explain what a subspace is and verify whether a given subset is one.

source_coverage.notes: Groups, fields, subspaces, spanning sets, basis and rank are developed with proofs in the book.

competencies.name: Matrices as linear mappings
competencies.why: Matrix multiplication is composition of transformations; without that reading, neural network layers are just index arithmetic.
outcomes: Given a linear mapping between specified spaces, write its matrix in a given basis and explain each entry.
Compute image and kernel of a mapping and interpret them geometrically.
Explain why the shape rules of matrix multiplication follow from function composition.

prerequisites.because: A mapping's matrix representation is defined relative to bases of the spaces it maps between.
Treating Ax=b as a mapping is only meaningful once the solution behaviour of systems is understood.

source_coverage.notes: Includes basis change and affine mappings, which are the prerequisite for understanding attention and normalisation layers.

competencies.name: Systems of linear equations and elimination
competencies.why: Solvability, uniqueness and numerical behaviour of linear systems decide whether a fitting procedure produces a usable answer.
outcomes: Solve a system by Gaussian elimination, stating the row operations used and the resulting solution set.
Classify a system as having no, one, or infinitely many solutions from its reduced row echelon form.
Explain what pivoting does and why the naive order of operations can fail numerically.

prerequisites.because: The solution set of a consistent system is described in the language of spans and subspaces.

supplemental_needed: Numerical stability of elimination and pivoting strategies beyond the book's brief remarks
source_coverage.notes: The book covers particular/general solutions, the minus-1 trick and algorithmic aspects; it does not develop floating-point analysis.

competencies.name: Norms, inner products and orthogonality
competencies.why: Loss functions, similarity measures and regularisation are all built from a choice of norm or inner product.
outcomes: Show that a candidate function is or is not an inner product by checking the defining properties.
Choose an appropriate norm for a stated problem and explain the consequences of the choice.
Compute the angle between two vectors and decide orthogonality.

prerequisites.because: Inner products are defined on vector spaces and induce the metric structure used throughout.

source_coverage.notes: Includes inner products of functions, which matters later for kernels.

competencies.name: Orthogonal projection and least squares geometry
competencies.why: Least squares, PCA and the attention mechanism are all projections onto subspaces; the geometry makes their properties visible.
outcomes: Derive the projection of a vector onto a subspace given a basis of that subspace.
Explain in geometric terms why the residual of a least-squares fit is orthogonal to the column space.
Derive the normal equations and state when they are a bad idea numerically.

prerequisites.because: Orthogonal projection is defined through the inner product.

supplemental_needed: QR and iterative solvers as practical alternatives to the normal equations
source_coverage.notes: The book derives projections in Chapter 3 and reuses them to interpret maximum-likelihood linear regression in Section 9.4.

competencies.name: Determinants, eigenvalues and eigenvectors
competencies.why: Eigenvalues describe how a transformation scales its invariant directions, which underpins stability, spectral methods and Hessian analysis.
outcomes: Compute eigenvalues and eigenvectors of a small matrix by hand and verify the result by substitution.
Explain what the determinant says about invertibility and volume scaling, including its sign.
Determine whether a matrix is diagonalisable and explain what failure to be diagonalisable means.

prerequisites.because: Eigenvectors are the directions a linear mapping preserves, so the mapping reading of matrices comes first.

competencies.name: Matrix decompositions
competencies.why: Decompositions expose structure that makes computation stable and interpretation possible.
outcomes: State the existence conditions of the Cholesky, eigendecomposition and SVD, and give an example that violates each condition.
Use the SVD to describe the action of a matrix as rotation, scaling and rotation.
Relate the eigendecomposition of a symmetric positive-definite matrix to its Cholesky factor.

prerequisites.because: Eigendecomposition is defined through eigenvalues and eigenvectors.
The SVD and Cholesky are stated in terms of orthonormal bases and positivity conditions.

supplemental_needed: Cost and stability comparison of the algorithms that compute these decompositions
source_coverage.notes: Section 4.7 (matrix phylogeny) is a synthesis of the conditions under which each decomposition exists.

competencies.name: Low-rank approximation and compression
competencies.why: Rank-truncated representations are how dimensionality reduction, model compression and latent-factor methods actually work.
outcomes: Derive the best rank-k approximation in the Frobenius norm from the SVD and state the size of the error.
Apply rank truncation to a data matrix and interpret the retained components.
Explain the trade-off between representation size and reconstruction error.

prerequisites.because: The Eckart-Young result is expressed in terms of the SVD.

competencies.name: Differentiation of scalar functions, gradients and linearisation
competencies.why: Learning is defined as minimising an objective, and derivatives are the local information that makes minimisation possible.
outcomes: Compute derivatives of composite scalar functions using the chain, product and quotient rules, showing intermediate steps.
Explain the derivative as a local linear approximation and use a Taylor expansion to bound the error of that approximation.
Compute the Hessian of a small function and classify its stationary points.

competencies.name: Gradients of vector- and matrix-valued functions
competencies.why: Model parameters are collected into vectors and matrices, so derivatives must be taken with respect to those objects and their shapes must be tracked.
outcomes: Given a function from matrices to vectors, write its Jacobian with correct shape and justify the layout convention used.
Apply the chain rule to a composition of matrix operations, tracking dimensions at each step.
Derive gradients of the standard least-squares and log-likelihood objectives from first principles.

prerequisites.because: The multivariate results are built on univariate differentiation and the chain rule.
Gradients with respect to parameters are expressed in the algebra of the spaces those parameters live in.

competencies.name: Backpropagation and automatic differentiation
competencies.why: Every deep-learning training run is executed by an automatic-differentiation engine; understanding it turns opaque failures into debuggable ones.
outcomes: Derive the backpropagation recurrence for a small feed-forward network by hand and check it numerically against finite differences.
Explain forward- versus reverse-mode differentiation and when each is preferable for a given input/output shape.
Diagnose a vanishing or exploding gradient by inspecting the propagation of terms.

prerequisites.because: Backpropagation is the chain rule applied in a particular evaluation order.

supplemental_needed: Reverse-mode implementation details in a modern framework, and memory/compute trade-offs of checkpointing
source_coverage.notes: The book derives gradients in a deep network and introduces automatic differentiation conceptually.

competencies.name: Probability spaces, random variables and distributions
competencies.why: Uncertainty is not an optional modelling choice; the axioms determine which claims about a model are well formed.
outcomes: Construct a probability space for a described random experiment and verify that the axioms hold.
Derive the density of a transformed random variable and state the assumptions the method requires.
Distinguish discrete from continuous models and explain why a density is not a probability.

competencies.name: Conditioning, Bayes' theorem and independence
competencies.why: Bayes' theorem is the formal rule for updating beliefs with evidence; conditioning errors are the most common probabilistic mistake in applied work.
outcomes: Apply the sum and product rules to a joint distribution to obtain marginals and conditionals, showing each step.
Distinguish independence from conditional independence and produce a counterexample where the two differ.
Explain the base-rate fallacy using a stated prior and likelihood.

prerequisites.because: Conditional probability is defined in terms of a probability space and a conditioning event of non-zero measure.

source_coverage.notes: Directed graphical models in Section 8.5 make conditional independence visible in a graph.

competencies.name: Expectation, covariance and the Gaussian distribution
competencies.why: Means, variances and covariance matrices are the summary statistics that most learning procedures operate on, and the Gaussian is the distribution they are usually derived from.
outcomes: Compute marginal and conditional means and covariances from a joint Gaussian and explain the result.
Prove that linear transformations of a Gaussian remain Gaussian, stating the conditions.
Explain why the covariance matrix must be symmetric positive semi-definite and what the eigendecomposition of it means.

prerequisites.because: Expectation and covariance are defined as integrals or sums over a probability model.
Marginals and conditionals of Gaussian vectors rely on the sum and product rules.

source_coverage.notes: Links directly to the Cholesky decomposition in MATH-07 through sampling and to PCA in ML-07.

competencies.name: Exponential family and conjugacy
competencies.why: Conjugate priors are why closed-form Bayesian updates exist for the models used in practice, and the exponential family explains which models have them.
outcomes: Write a given distribution in exponential-family form and identify its sufficient statistics.
Select a conjugate prior for a stated likelihood and derive the posterior parameters.
Explain what the posterior update is doing in terms of prior pseudo-observations.

prerequisites.because: Conjugate pairs are stated through the natural parameters of the family and are exercised on the Gaussian and categorical cases.

supplemental_needed: Practical consequences for Bayesian model implementation, such as when closed forms disappear
source_coverage.notes: Marked working rather than deep: engineers need to recognise and use conjugacy, and to know its limits, more often than they need to re-derive the family's algebra.

competencies.name: Gradient-based optimisation
competencies.why: Training is optimisation; learning-rate behaviour, divergence and slow convergence are optimisation phenomena, not framework bugs.
outcomes: Derive the gradient-descent update and explain why the negative gradient direction is the direction of steepest local decrease.
Demonstrate divergence by choosing a learning rate too large for a given objective, and explain the condition that governs it.
Compare batch, mini-batch and stochastic updates in terms of gradient variance and runtime.

prerequisites.because: The update rule requires the gradient of the objective with respect to the parameters.

supplemental_needed: Adaptive and momentum methods, which are the default in practice and are only referenced in the book

competencies.name: Convexity and constrained optimisation
competencies.why: Convexity is the assumption behind the guarantee that a found minimum is global, and duality is the machinery behind support vector machines and much of applied optimisation.
outcomes: Determine whether a stated function is convex using the definition and the first- or second-order conditions.
Form the Lagrangian of a constrained problem and interpret the KKT conditions and the meaning of the multipliers.
Explain weak and strong duality and the conditions under which they coincide.

prerequisites.because: Constrained optimisation is introduced as an extension of unconstrained gradient methods.
Second-order convexity conditions are read off the Hessian's eigenvalues.

supplemental_needed: Interior-point and other solver families beyond the book's introductive treatment
source_coverage.notes: The dual SVM derivation in Section 12.3 is the applied payoff of this competency.

competencies.name: Statistical estimation and model selection
competencies.why: Maximum likelihood, maximum a posteriori and Bayesian inference are the three ways parameter estimates are produced, and each changes what you are entitled to claim.
outcomes: Derive the maximum-likelihood estimate for a stated model and check the second-order condition for a maximum.
Show how a Gaussian prior on the parameters turns maximum a posteriori estimation into regularised least squares.
Compare point estimation with Bayesian inference in terms of computational cost and the information retained.

prerequisites.because: Estimation is posed over a probabilistic model with likelihoods built from the distributions studied there.
Posterior computation is Bayes' theorem.

supplemental_needed: Approximate inference methods named but not developed in the book (Laplace approximation, variational inference, MCMC)

competencies.name: Numerical stability, conditioning and floating-point behaviour
competencies.why: The difference between a method that works on paper and one that works on a computer is conditioning, precision and algorithm cost.
outcomes: Estimate the cost of a stated matrix operation in floating-point operations and say when a factorised form is preferable.
Identify a numerically unstable formulation of a standard computation and replace it with a stable one.
Explain what the condition number of a matrix measures and the consequences for solving a system.

prerequisites.because: Error behaviour is studied on the elimination and least-squares procedures already understood.
Stability arguments are made about factorisations.

supplemental_needed: A numerical-linear-algebra reference covering floating-point analysis, condition numbers, pivoting and the cost of decompositions
source_coverage.notes: The supplied book mentions stability and complexity at several points but does not teach the analysis. Treat as a real gap rather than stretching the book's coverage.

competencies.name: Python language fundamentals and idioms
competencies.why: Python is the working language of nearly every AI role, and its idioms differ from those of the languages most learners arrive from.
outcomes: Write a program of moderate size using functions, comprehensions, generators and context managers appropriately.
Explain Python's name binding and mutability rules and predict the output of a short snippet involving both.
Use virtual environments and a dependency manifest to make a project reproducible.

supplemental_needed: A programming source (roadmap nominates Python Crash Course; the free Harvard CS50P and one paid course are also recorded)
source_coverage.notes: Awaiting the user's source material.

competencies.name: Modular design and the Python data model
competencies.why: Code that has to be read, tested and extended later needs explicit boundaries; design patterns are tools for that, not decoration.
outcomes: Decompose a stated problem into modules with clear responsibilities and justify the boundaries.
Implement the same behaviour through composition and through inheritance and explain when each is preferable.
Apply a named design pattern to a concrete problem and justify why it fits.

prerequisites.because: Language features such as classes, protocols and dataclasses are the vocabulary design patterns are written in.

supplemental_needed: A design-patterns source for Python (object-oriented and functional styles)
source_coverage.notes: Awaiting sources.

competencies.name: Error handling, debugging and logging
competencies.why: Failing clearly and diagnosing quickly is a larger part of professional work than writing new code.
outcomes: Distinguish recoverable from unrecoverable errors in a stated component and handle each accordingly.
Use a debugger to locate a defect and explain the state of the program at each step.
Instrument a program with structured logs that would let someone else diagnose a failure without reproducing it.

prerequisites.because: Exceptions, tracebacks and module structure are language-level material.

supplemental_needed: A source covering Python exception design, the standard debugger and structured logging
source_coverage.notes: Awaiting sources.

competencies.name: Environments, packaging and the shell
competencies.why: Reproducing your own results a month later depends on controlling interpreters, dependencies and the command line.
outcomes: Create an isolated environment, pin dependencies and reproduce it from a lock file.
Use the shell to inspect, filter and combine files and processes, including pipes and exit codes.
Explain what happens at process startup, including how the interpreter finds imports.

prerequisites.because: The environment mechanics only matter once there is a program to run.

supplemental_needed: Shell and Linux material, plus packaging tooling documentation
source_coverage.notes: Awaiting sources.

competencies.name: Testing and test-driven development
competencies.why: Tests are the mechanism by which a claim about code becomes checkable, including for numerical code where correctness is not binary.
outcomes: Write unit tests that fail for the right reason before the implementation exists.
Choose an assertion strategy for floating-point results and justify the tolerance.
Explain the difference between unit, integration and end-to-end tests and place a given test correctly.

prerequisites.because: Tests are written in the language being tested.
Testing numerical code requires understanding tolerance and conditioning.

supplemental_needed: A testing source covering pytest and property-based testing
source_coverage.notes: Awaiting sources. Note that the supplied book's exercise sets have no solutions, which is a separate verification problem for our own exercises.

competencies.name: Concurrency, parallelism and asynchrony
competencies.why: Data loading, serving and evaluation are all dominated by waiting; the wrong concurrency model wastes most of the available throughput.
outcomes: Choose between threads, processes and asynchronous I/O for a stated workload and justify the choice using the GIL and the shape of the work.
Write a program that bounds concurrency explicitly and handles partial failure.
Measure whether a concurrency change improved throughput and explain the result.

prerequisites.because: Concurrency constructs are language features.
Concurrent work introduces failure modes that must be handled and observed.

supplemental_needed: Python concurrency material (asyncio, threading, multiprocessing) matching the current interpreter version
source_coverage.notes: Awaiting sources.

competencies.name: Version control and collaborative workflow
competencies.why: Every artefact of this platform, and of any real project, is managed through version control, including the reviewing of other people's changes.
outcomes: Perform a branch, merge and rebase workflow and explain how the resulting history differs.
Resolve a merge conflict deliberately rather than by choosing one side wholesale.
Review a change and give feedback that distinguishes correctness, style and design concerns.

supplemental_needed: A Git reference (the roadmap nominates Pro Git) plus the interactive branching tutorial
source_coverage.notes: Awaiting sources.

competencies.name: Functional programming tools in Python
competencies.why: Mapping, filtering, reducing and immutability reduce whole classes of bugs in data-processing code.
outcomes: Rewrite a stated imperative loop as a generator pipeline and compare readability and memory behaviour.
Explain the trade-offs between mutation and returning new structures in a data pipeline.
Use a functional style where it clarifies the transformation and say where it does not.

prerequisites.because: Comprehensions, generators and closures are language features.

supplemental_needed: Python functional-programming material
source_coverage.notes: Awaiting sources.

competencies.name: Core data structures and their complexity
competencies.why: Choosing the wrong container is one of the most common causes of slow code, and it is a standard interview screen.
outcomes: Select an appropriate data structure for a stated access pattern and justify it with complexity reasoning.
Implement a hash map and a balanced-tree-backed map conceptually and explain when each degrades.
Analyse the memory cost of a given structure at a stated scale.

prerequisites.because: The structures are implemented and used in Python.

supplemental_needed: A data-structures source, plus practice problems
source_coverage.notes: Awaiting sources.

competencies.name: Algorithm design paradigms and complexity analysis
competencies.why: Complexity analysis predicts whether a pipeline or training loop will finish, before it is run at scale.
outcomes: Derive the time and space complexity of a stated algorithm, including the amortised case where relevant.
Choose between a greedy, divide-and-conquer and dynamic-programming formulation for a stated problem and justify the choice.
Identify the dominant cost in a data-processing pipeline by analysis and confirm it by measurement.

prerequisites.because: Complexity is analysed on concrete structures.

supplemental_needed: An algorithms source and a problem-practice schedule
source_coverage.notes: Awaiting sources.

competencies.name: Vectorised numeric computing
competencies.why: Almost all machine-learning computation is expressed as array operations whose performance and correctness depend on shape and broadcasting rules.
outcomes: Express a stated computation as array operations without Python loops and explain the broadcasting involved.
Predict the output shape of an expression involving broadcasting and catch a silent shape bug.
Measure the difference between a loop and a vectorised implementation and explain the cost model.

prerequisites.because: Array operations are matrix algebra; understanding the algebra is what makes them expressible.
Floating-point behaviour and accumulation order matter in vectorised code.

supplemental_needed: NumPy documentation and exercises
source_coverage.notes: The supplied book uses array notation but does not teach the library. Awaiting sources for the tooling.

competencies.name: Implementing learning algorithms from first principles
competencies.why: Implementing an algorithm once from its mathematics is what converts a definition into understanding, and it is the fastest way to find out whether you actually followed the derivation.
outcomes: Implement a stated algorithm from its mathematical description without consulting a library implementation, and verify it against a known result.
Validate the implementation by gradient checking and by comparison with a reference library.
Explain any deviation found between the implementation and the reference.

prerequisites.because: The derived gradients are the specification.
The implementation is code.
Verification against reference results is a testing skill.

supplemental_needed: None for the mathematics; the exercises must be authored, since the source's own exercise sets have no supplied solutions
source_coverage.notes: This is where the supplied book's exercise sets (chapters 2-7) become usable as specifications for implementation work.

competencies.name: SQL and query reasoning
competencies.why: Almost all data access in a production system ends in a query, and query correctness is a reasoning skill rather than a syntax skill.
outcomes: Write a query using joins, grouping and window functions and explain the evaluation order of the clauses.
Predict the effect of a join condition on row counts and detect an unintended duplication.
Read a query plan and identify the step that dominates cost.

supplemental_needed: A SQL source with real datasets (roadmap nominates Practical SQL, plus the SQLZoo and Mode tutorials)
source_coverage.notes: Awaiting sources.

competencies.name: Relational and dimensional data modelling
competencies.why: The shape of the data model determines which questions can be answered cheaply and which become ambiguous.
outcomes: Model a stated business process as facts and dimensions and justify the grain.
Explain slowly changing dimension handling and choose a strategy for a stated requirement.
Identify a normalisation anomaly in a proposed schema and propose a fix.

prerequisites.because: Dimensional modelling is expressed as and evaluated through queries.

supplemental_needed: A dimensional-modelling source (the roadmap nominates Kimball-style material)
source_coverage.notes: Awaiting sources.

competencies.name: Batch pipelines and ETL/ELT design
competencies.why: Most production data defects originate in the pipeline rather than in the model.
outcomes: Design an incremental batch pipeline with explicit handling of late and duplicate data.
Explain the difference between transformation-in-warehouse and transformation-before-load and choose appropriately.
Make a pipeline rerunnable and idempotent and demonstrate that property with a test.

prerequisites.because: Transformations are expressed as queries.
Pipeline failures must be observable and recoverable.

supplemental_needed: An ELT/ETL source and orchestration tooling documentation
source_coverage.notes: Awaiting sources.

competencies.name: Workflow orchestration and scheduling
competencies.why: Production data work is a dependency graph running on a schedule, with failure and backfill as normal cases.
outcomes: Express a stated workflow as a directed acyclic graph with explicit dependencies and retry policy.
Explain how a backfill is performed without corrupting already-produced results.
Diagnose a schedule that silently stopped producing data.

prerequisites.because: Orchestration schedules the pipeline that already exists.

supplemental_needed: Airflow or equivalent orchestration documentation
source_coverage.notes: Awaiting sources.

competencies.name: Distributed batch processing
competencies.why: Data that does not fit on one machine requires reasoning about partitioning and shuffles rather than about Python.
outcomes: Explain how a stated distributed transformation partitions data and where a shuffle occurs.
Diagnose a job whose runtime is dominated by a data skew rather than by volume.
Choose between the available partitioning and join strategies for a stated dataset shape.

prerequisites.because: Distribution introduces the same failure and scheduling issues as concurrency, at a larger scale.
The distributed engine executes the pipeline being designed.

supplemental_needed: Spark documentation and hands-on datasets
source_coverage.notes: Awaiting sources.

competencies.name: Streaming data systems
competencies.why: Event-driven systems change the correctness question from 'is the batch complete' to 'how do I reason about time'.
outcomes: Explain event time versus processing time and the consequence for a stated computation.
Describe how a stream processor maintains state and what happens to it after a restart.
Choose delivery semantics for a stated requirement and state the cost.

prerequisites.because: Streaming systems reuse the partitioning and distribution model.

supplemental_needed: Streaming material covering event time, windowing and delivery guarantees
source_coverage.notes: Awaiting sources.

competencies.name: NoSQL and storage-engine selection
competencies.why: Choosing a storage engine is choosing a consistency and access model, and the wrong choice cannot be fixed later.
outcomes: Compare two storage families for a stated access pattern against the CAP-style trade-offs.
Design a document or key-value schema for a stated query workload and identify the queries it cannot serve.
Explain what the chosen consistency level means for a stated read path.

prerequisites.because: The trade-off is only meaningful against one's modelling needs.

supplemental_needed: A source covering document, key-value, wide-column and graph stores
source_coverage.notes: Awaiting sources.

competencies.name: Data quality, validation and contracts
competencies.why: A model cannot be more trustworthy than the data it was fitted on, and silent data breaks are the most expensive failures in ML systems.
outcomes: Specify the assumptions a dataset must satisfy for a stated use, as executable checks.
Detect distribution change between training and serving data and state whether it matters for the decision made.
Design a validation gate that blocks promotion of bad data and explain what it cannot catch.

prerequisites.because: Validation is implemented as queries or dataframe assertions.
Quantifying distribution change requires the summary statistics studied there.

supplemental_needed: Data-validation tooling and drift-detection methods
source_coverage.notes: The supplied book discusses data and models conceptually in Section 8.1 but is not a data-engineering source; the honest classification is partial, and the tooling gap is real.

competencies.name: Lakehouse and table formats
competencies.why: Open table formats change what is possible on cheap storage: transactions, schema evolution and time travel on top of object stores.
outcomes: Explain what a table format adds on top of Parquet files in a bucket.
Describe how time travel and schema evolution are supported and their cost.
Choose between a warehouse, a lake and a lakehouse table for a stated workload.

prerequisites.because: The formats manage the tables the pipelines write.
The query engines that read these tables are distributed.

supplemental_needed: Documentation for an open table format and its concurrency model
source_coverage.notes: Awaiting sources. Very version-sensitive: any lesson must record the format version it describes.

competencies.name: Cloud platforms for data and ML
competencies.why: The platform supplies identity, storage, compute and networking, and misconfiguring them is both a cost and a security problem.
outcomes: Sketch the minimal infrastructure for a stated workload using managed services and identify the cost drivers.
Explain the identity model used to grant a service access to a data store.
Distinguish which failures are the platform's responsibility and which are the engineer's.

prerequisites.because: Managed services are chosen against storage and access requirements.
Cloud access control is application security in a different vocabulary.

supplemental_needed: Official cloud documentation for one provider, dated, plus a cost-modelling exercise
source_coverage.notes: Awaiting sources. Roadmap lists this as a single skill covering three providers; the competency is deliberately provider-agnostic so that lessons can be written for whichever the user has access to.

competencies.name: Service and API design
competencies.why: An ML capability becomes useful only when another system can call it under load and get an answer it can act on.
outcomes: Design a REST or RPC interface for a stated capability, including error semantics and idempotency.
Explain the difference between a synchronous and an asynchronous design for a stated latency budget.
Document an interface so that a consumer can use it without reading the implementation.

prerequisites.because: Service boundaries are a modular-design decision.

supplemental_needed: Web framework documentation (the roadmap nominates FastAPI or Django) and an API-design reference
source_coverage.notes: Awaiting sources.

competencies.name: Containers and reproducible runtime environments
competencies.why: A container is the unit in which a model, its dependencies and its runtime configuration travel together.
outcomes: Write a container definition that builds deterministically and explain each layer's purpose.
Diagnose a mismatch between local and containerised behaviour.
State what a container does not isolate, and the consequence for security and resource limits.

prerequisites.because: Containerisation formalises the dependency-management problem.

supplemental_needed: Docker documentation and an exercise on reproducing a training environment
source_coverage.notes: Awaiting sources.

competencies.name: Continuous integration and delivery
competencies.why: Automatic checking is what makes it possible to keep changing a system without breaking it, including the educational content in this repository.
outcomes: Design a pipeline that runs the relevant checks on each change and fails for the right reason.
Explain which checks belong before merge and which belong after, and why.
Make a change that requires a data migration deployable without downtime.

prerequisites.because: Continuous integration is the automated execution of the tests already written.
The pipeline is triggered by the version-control workflow.

supplemental_needed: CI/CD documentation and a worked pipeline
source_coverage.notes: Awaiting sources. The platform's own content pipeline is a legitimate exercise for this competency.

competencies.name: Application security and authentication
competencies.why: Every deployed AI capability is an attack surface, and the failure of the most common web vulnerabilities is not subtle.
outcomes: Identify the OWASP-class vulnerability present in a given code sample and fix it.
Explain the difference between authentication and authorisation and implement an authorisation check on the server.
Describe how secrets should be supplied to a running service.

prerequisites.because: The vulnerabilities are situated in the interface being built.

supplemental_needed: OWASP material and framework authentication documentation
source_coverage.notes: Awaiting sources.

competencies.name: Distributed systems reasoning
competencies.why: Anything that has to survive a machine disappearing is a distributed system, whether or not it was designed as one.
outcomes: Explain the failure models (crash, partition, latency) and how each changes a design.
Reason about consistency and availability trade-offs for a stated service.
Design retry, timeout and idempotency behaviour together rather than separately.

prerequisites.because: The reasoning is applied to service interactions.
Concurrency thinking is the local version of these problems.

supplemental_needed: A distributed-systems source; the roadmap places this in the specialisation phase
source_coverage.notes: Awaiting sources. Classified as role-dependent rather than universal: essential for serving infrastructure, less so for application-layer AI engineering.

competencies.name: System design for AI applications
competencies.why: The interview and the job both ask for a defensible end-to-end design, not a list of components.
outcomes: Produce a design for a stated AI feature covering data flow, failure handling, evaluation and cost, with the trade-offs stated explicitly.
Estimate the capacity requirements of a stated design and identify the binding constraint.
Critique a proposed design and name the assumption most likely to be wrong.

prerequisites.because: Design work is expressed through interfaces.
The design must include the operational lifecycle of whatever is built.

supplemental_needed: System-design material plus AI-specific case studies
source_coverage.notes: Awaiting sources; case studies will be authored as original scenarios with rubrics.

competencies.name: Container orchestration and deployment operations
competencies.why: Serving a model at varying load requires scheduling, scaling and rollout control that a single container cannot provide.
outcomes: Deploy a service with declarative configuration and explain how the scheduler places it.
Configure resource requests and limits and predict the scheduling consequence of each.
Perform and roll back a versioned rollout.

prerequisites.because: Orchestration schedules the containers already defined.
Rollouts are triggered and gated by the delivery pipeline.

supplemental_needed: Kubernetes documentation and a local-cluster exercise
source_coverage.notes: Awaiting sources. Role-dependent: important for platform-facing roles.

competencies.name: Problem formulation and baselines
competencies.why: A model is only meaningful relative to a decision, a loss and a baseline; without those, a metric is just a number.
outcomes: Translate a stated business objective into a learning problem with an explicit target, loss and evaluation protocol.
Establish a trivial baseline and state what a model must beat to be worth deploying.
Identify the sampling unit and explain how it constrains validation.

prerequisites.because: Formulating a learning problem requires knowing what a model and its parameters are.

supplemental_needed: Business-objective translation and metric selection from an applied-ML source; the book is mathematical and stops at the loss function
source_coverage.notes: The empirical-risk framing in Section 8.2 is the mathematical core of this competency.

competencies.name: Supervised learning algorithms
competencies.why: Choosing between linear regression, a margin-based classifier, a tree ensemble or a network is a decision with consequences that must be reasoned about.
outcomes: Derive the objective of a stated supervised method, state its assumptions, and solve a small instance by hand.
Compare two methods on a stated dataset and explain the difference in terms of the inductive bias of each.
Explain what a kernel does and when a linear method becomes a nonlinear one.

prerequisites.because: The methods are estimation procedures on a probabilistic or loss-based objective.
Margin maximisation and regularisation are constrained-optimisation problems.

supplemental_needed: Tree-based ensembles, nearest-neighbour methods, and the applied comparison of classifiers; the book covers regression and SVM only
source_coverage.notes: The book's coverage is deep but narrow: linear regression and SVM are developed thoroughly, and everything else in the classical toolbox must come from another source.

competencies.name: Evaluation metrics and their limitations
competencies.why: Every metric encodes a value judgement, and an inappropriate metric produces a model that is good at the wrong thing.
outcomes: Choose a metric for a stated error-cost structure and justify the choice against at least one alternative.
Construct a dataset on which a stated metric gives a misleading answer.
Explain the trade-off between precision and recall for a stated decision threshold.

prerequisites.because: Metrics only mean something relative to the decision they support.
Probabilistic classification output requires conditional-probability reasoning.

supplemental_needed: Calibration, ranking metrics, imbalanced-data metrics and class-threshold selection
source_coverage.notes: The book supplies the loss-function view (expected risk) but not the applied metric catalogue.

competencies.name: Validation methodology and leakage
competencies.why: Most reported improvements that do not survive deployment are caused by evaluation that leaked information.
outcomes: Design a validation split appropriate to the data's structure and state what it protects against.
Identify a leakage path in a stated pipeline and demonstrate the inflated score it produces.
Explain nested cross-validation and when the extra loop is necessary.

prerequisites.because: Splitting is only definable once the sampling unit and objective are fixed.
Model selection is framed as estimating generalisation performance.

supplemental_needed: Grouped, stratified and temporal splitting for real data structures
source_coverage.notes: Section 8.6 develops nested cross-validation and Bayesian model selection; the temporal and grouped cases are a genuine addition.

competencies.name: Feature engineering and preprocessing
competencies.why: The transformation applied to inputs often matters more than the choice of algorithm.
outcomes: Design transformations for a stated feature type and justify each against alternatives.
Explain why a transformation must be fitted on training data only and demonstrate the failure when it is not.
Diagnose a preprocessing step that destroys information needed by the model.

prerequisites.because: Features are chosen for a defined learning problem.
Preprocessing is where data-quality problems become model problems.

supplemental_needed: Categorical encoding, scaling, text and time features; the book's treatment is mathematical rather than practical

competencies.name: Generalisation, regularisation and the bias-variance trade-off
competencies.why: The difference between fitting data and learning from it is the central problem of the field.
outcomes: Explain underfitting and overfitting in terms of the decomposition of expected error.
Derive how a prior on the parameters becomes a penalty term and predict its effect on the fitted solution.
Select a regularisation strength using validation evidence rather than intuition.

prerequisites.because: Regularisation is derived from maximum a posteriori estimation.
The effect of regularisation can only be measured on held-out data.

source_coverage.notes: Section 9.2.4 (MAP estimation as regularisation) is the explicit bridge from the mathematics to the practice.

competencies.name: Unsupervised learning and latent-variable models
competencies.why: Structure discovery, compression and density estimation are needed when there is no label to fit.
outcomes: Derive PCA from the maximum-variance and reconstruction-error formulations and show that they agree.
Explain the expectation-maximisation algorithm for a mixture model and what it converges to.
Choose between dimensionality reduction and clustering for a stated exploratory question.

prerequisites.because: PCA is a low-rank approximation problem.
Latent-variable models are fitted by maximum likelihood.

supplemental_needed: Practical cluster validation and the operational use of dimensionality reduction
source_coverage.notes: Two full chapters of the source are devoted to this competency, which makes it one of the best-supported topics for a first module.

competencies.name: Experiment tracking and reproducibility
competencies.why: An experiment that cannot be reproduced cannot be built upon, and 'it worked last week' is not evidence.
outcomes: Record the inputs, configuration and outputs of an experiment such that it can be re-run exactly.
Explain which sources of nondeterminism exist in a stated training pipeline and how to control them.
Compare two experiment runs and attribute the difference to a specific change.

prerequisites.because: Reproducibility depends on versioning code and configuration.
The comparison is only meaningful with a valid evaluation protocol.

supplemental_needed: Experiment-tracking tooling documentation and a reproducibility exercise
source_coverage.notes: Awaiting sources.

competencies.name: Neural network fundamentals
competencies.why: A network is a composition of parameterised functions trained by gradient descent; without that reading, architecture diagrams are not interpretable.
outcomes: Write the forward computation of a small network explicitly as matrix operations and derive its parameter gradients.
Explain why a nonlinearity is required and what each common activation does to the gradient.
Compute the parameter count and the forward-pass cost of a stated architecture.

prerequisites.because: Training the network requires the backpropagation machinery.
The parameters are updated by a gradient-based optimiser.

supplemental_needed: A deep-learning source covering architecture, training practice, activations and regularisation for networks
source_coverage.notes: The book supplies the mathematics of gradients and the network notation in Section 5.6.1 but is deliberately not a deep-learning text; the classification of partial is therefore honest rather than generous.

competencies.name: Training dynamics and optimisation for deep networks
competencies.why: Whether a model trains is governed by learning rates, initialisation, batch size and the shape of the loss surface.
outcomes: Diagnose a training run from its loss curves and name the most likely cause of the observed behaviour.
Explain what momentum and adaptive step sizes change relative to plain gradient descent.
Design a learning-rate schedule for a stated training budget and justify it.

prerequisites.because: The dynamics are the behaviour of the network's optimisation.
The methods are extensions of the gradient-descent family.

supplemental_needed: A deep-learning source with an empirical treatment of optimisers, schedules and initialisation
source_coverage.notes: The supplied book's optimisation chapter is about continuous optimisation in general, not about training deep networks; claiming otherwise would be wrong.

competencies.name: Deep learning frameworks and the training loop
competencies.why: The framework is where the mathematics becomes a running system, including automatic differentiation, devices and data loading.
outcomes: Implement and train a stated model in a framework, explaining what each part of the training loop does.
Explain how automatic differentiation in the framework relates to the backpropagation derivation.
Diagnose a runtime shape or device mismatch and fix it at the source.

prerequisites.because: The framework implements the model whose mathematics is already understood.
Framework tensors follow the same broadcasting and shape rules.

supplemental_needed: PyTorch documentation and guided practice (the roadmap nominates PyTorch as a skill of its own)
source_coverage.notes: Awaiting sources. Version-sensitive: lessons must record the framework version they were checked against.

competencies.name: Convolutional networks and computer vision
competencies.why: Vision models are the clearest case of architecture encoding an assumption about the data, which makes the inductive-bias reasoning transferable.
outcomes: Explain how a convolution exploits spatial structure and compute the output shape for stated parameters.
Compare a convolutional architecture with a fully connected one on the same task and explain the difference in parameters and accuracy.
Diagnose a vision pipeline whose preprocessing differs between training and inference.

prerequisites.because: Convolutions are layers within the network formalism.
Image pipelines are preprocessing pipelines.

supplemental_needed: A computer-vision source covering convolutional architectures, augmentation and transfer learning
source_coverage.notes: Awaiting sources. Classified as a specialisation: essential for vision roles, optional for language-focused paths.

competencies.name: Sequence modelling and attention
competencies.why: Attention is the mechanism behind current language systems, and it is a learned, differentiable lookup rather than a mystery.
outcomes: Describe the recurrent approach to sequences and explain why it struggles with long-range dependencies.
Compute the attention output for a small set of queries, keys and values by hand.
Explain multi-head attention and the role of scaling in the softmax.

prerequisites.because: Attention is a composition of linear maps and softmax inside a network.
Attention scores are inner products, and their interpretation is geometric.

supplemental_needed: A transformer reference: the original attention paper and a reputable architectural walkthrough, dated
source_coverage.notes: The book supplies the inner-product and projection machinery needed, and nothing about attention itself. The partial classification reflects that precisely.

competencies.name: Transformer architecture and language models
competencies.why: The transformer is the architecture current language systems are built on, and its components each exist for a reason that can be explained.
outcomes: Describe the role of each component of a transformer block and what breaks when one is removed.
Explain positional encoding and why attention alone is permutation-equivariant.
Trace the shape of the data through a stated transformer configuration.

prerequisites.because: The transformer is assembled from attention, normalisation and feed-forward components.

supplemental_needed: Primary references for the transformer and for a current open model's configuration; both dated and version-recorded
source_coverage.notes: No supplied source covers this. It is a first-class gap, not a minor one.

competencies.name: Pre-training, fine-tuning and parameter-efficient adaptation
competencies.why: Choosing between prompting, retrieval and weight updates is an engineering decision about cost, data and control.
outcomes: Distinguish pre-training, supervised fine-tuning and parameter-efficient adaptation in terms of what changes and what it costs.
Select an adaptation strategy for a stated constraint set and justify it.
Explain what catastrophic forgetting is and how data mixture affects it.

prerequisites.because: Adaptation is performed on a transformer whose parts are understood.
Whatever is adapted is adapted by gradient-based optimisation.

supplemental_needed: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning literature and framework documentation, dated
source_coverage.notes: Awaiting sources. Fast-moving: lessons must state the model and library versions they describe and record when they were checked.

competencies.name: Distributed and efficient training
competencies.why: Model and data scale determine which parallelism strategy is even possible, and the constraint is memory before it is compute.
outcomes: Explain the difference between data, tensor and pipeline parallelism in terms of what is communicated.
Estimate whether a stated model fits on stated hardware and identify the limiting resource.
Apply a memory-reduction technique and explain its effect on compute.

prerequisites.because: Distribution changes the optimisation dynamics and the meaning of batch size.
Distributed training is a distributed-systems problem.

supplemental_needed: Distributed-training documentation and a memory-accounting exercise
source_coverage.notes: Classified as a specialisation with awareness as the initial target: most AI engineering roles consume the results of this work rather than perform it.

competencies.name: How large language models behave
competencies.why: Predicting the next token explains the characteristic failures, the cost structure and why evaluation is hard.
outcomes: Explain tokenisation and its consequences for arithmetic, spelling and multilingual behaviour.
Describe the sampling parameters of a generation call and predict how each changes the output.
Identify a task that a next-token predictor structurally cannot perform reliably and explain why.

prerequisites.because: The behaviour follows from the architecture, training objective and decoding procedure.

supplemental_needed: Model-behaviour documentation and empirical exercises against a stated model version
source_coverage.notes: Awaiting sources.

competencies.name: Prompting and context engineering
competencies.why: The context window is the only interface an application has to steer the model, and its allocation is an engineering budget.
outcomes: Design a prompt for a stated task with explicit output contract, worked examples and failure handling.
Measure the effect of a prompt change on a held-out set rather than on inspection of one output.
Allocate a fixed context budget across instructions, retrieved evidence and history, and justify the allocation.

prerequisites.because: Prompt effectiveness depends on how the model processes its input.

supplemental_needed: Provider documentation current at the time of writing, plus evaluation harness practice
source_coverage.notes: The roadmap lists no separate prompting skill; the audit adds this competency because it is what most 'AI engineer' postings screen for. Recorded as an addition with rationale rather than a roadmap topic.

competencies.name: Retrieval-augmented generation and vector search
competencies.why: Retrieval is how a system uses knowledge it was not trained on, and its failures are traceable to retrieval before generation.
outcomes: Explain the components of a retrieval pipeline and the decision each one makes.
Diagnose whether a wrong answer came from retrieval or from generation, with evidence.
Compare embedding- and keyword-based retrieval for a stated query distribution and choose deliberately.

prerequisites.because: Retrieved evidence has to be placed in the context to be used.
Embedding similarity is an inner-product or distance computation in a vector space.
Retrieval is only as good as the corpus and its validation.

supplemental_needed: Vector-search documentation, embedding-model documentation, and evaluation methods for retrieval
source_coverage.notes: Awaiting sources. The supplied book's inner-product and projection chapters give the mathematical foundation but not the system.

competencies.name: Evaluating and guarding generative systems
competencies.why: Generative outputs are not single labels, so evaluation must be designed rather than computed, and unsupported claims must be caught before a user sees them.
outcomes: Design an evaluation for a stated generative task with a reference set and a stated agreement target between graders.
Explain the failure modes of model-as-judge evaluation and control for at least one.
Specify a guardrail for a named risk and state the false-positive cost it introduces.

prerequisites.because: What is evaluated is model behaviour.
Metric design and its limitations are the same discipline applied to a new output type.

supplemental_needed: Evaluation methodology for free-form outputs, and safety guidance from a reputable source
source_coverage.notes: Awaiting sources. This competency is the reason the platform's own verification design is documented so carefully: the same problem appears here.

competencies.name: Agents and tool use
competencies.why: Once a model can call tools, the engineering problem changes from text generation to control flow with unreliable components.
outcomes: Design a control loop for a stated task and specify the termination and failure conditions.
Explain how tool schemas constrain model behaviour and where the loop can fail unboundedly.
Bound the cost and the blast radius of an agent acting on a stated system.

prerequisites.because: Tool calls are produced through the same interface.
Failures in a loop with external effects are distributed-systems and security problems.

supplemental_needed: Tool-use documentation and case studies with explicit failure analysis
source_coverage.notes: Awaiting sources. Kept at working level: the area is unsettled and lessons must not present one framework's style as settled practice.

competencies.name: Cost, latency and context management
competencies.why: For generative systems, unit economics and latency are product constraints as much as engineering ones.
outcomes: Estimate the cost and latency of a stated pipeline from token counts and model pricing, with the assumptions written down.
Reduce the cost of a stated pipeline and demonstrate that quality was preserved.
Explain caching and batching opportunities and the correctness conditions each requires.

prerequisites.because: Context size is the principal cost driver and is controlled by prompt design.
This is the generative-AI instance of cost engineering.

supplemental_needed: Current provider pricing and latency documentation, dated, plus a measurement exercise
source_coverage.notes: Awaiting sources. Any price figure in a lesson must be dated and treated as an example, never as a fact.

competencies.name: ML lifecycle and MLOps principles
competencies.why: The lifecycle, not the model, is what a team operates; without it, work is repeated and results are not comparable.
outcomes: Describe the stages of the lifecycle for a stated system and name the artifact produced by each.
Explain versioning, automation and monitoring as separable concerns and how each fails.
Choose a maturity level appropriate to a stated team and justify not doing more.

prerequisites.because: Experiment tracking is the first lifecycle component, at the smallest scale.
Automation of the lifecycle reuses the delivery pipeline.

supplemental_needed: MLOps principles and reference architecture, from a primary source such as the MLOps literature and current platform documentation
source_coverage.notes: Awaiting sources. The audit treats production engineering as the largest gap between the two roadmaps as written and what the roles described in the references actually screen for.

competencies.name: Model serving and deployment patterns
competencies.why: Deployment is where a model meets its latency budget, its batch size and its failure behaviour.
outcomes: Choose between batch, real-time and streaming inference for a stated requirement and justify it.
Explain the trade-offs between constructing the request-time features and precomputing them.
Design a safe release process for a model change, including rollback.

prerequisites.because: Serving is one stage of the lifecycle.
Serving is an interface with a latency contract.

supplemental_needed: Serving framework documentation and a latency/throughput measurement exercise
source_coverage.notes: Awaiting sources.

competencies.name: Monitoring, drift detection and observability
competencies.why: A deployed model degrades silently; only instrumentation makes degradation visible before users report it.
outcomes: Define the signals that indicate a stated system is degrading, separating input, output and outcome signals.
Explain the difficulty of monitoring when labels arrive late or never, and propose a proxy with its limitation.
Design an alert with a threshold chosen from measured behaviour rather than intuition.

prerequisites.because: There is nothing to monitor until the system is served.
Input-drift detection is data validation applied over time.

supplemental_needed: Observability tooling documentation and drift-detection methods
source_coverage.notes: Awaiting sources.

competencies.name: Reliability, incident response and debugging in production
competencies.why: Systems fail in ways that local testing does not reproduce, and the response determines the cost of the failure.
outcomes: Write a runbook for a stated failure mode that a colleague could follow without the author present.
Distinguish a symptom from a cause during a stated incident and describe the diagnostic sequence.
Produce a blameless post-mortem with actions that address the cause.

prerequisites.because: Diagnosis requires the signals monitoring provides.
Most production failures are interaction failures between components.

supplemental_needed: Site-reliability material and incident-review practice
source_coverage.notes: Awaiting sources.

competencies.name: Security, privacy and governance for AI systems
competencies.why: AI systems process data with legal and ethical constraints, and the failure modes include prompt injection as well as classic data exposure.
outcomes: Identify the trust boundaries in a stated AI system and the data that crosses each.
Explain prompt injection and design a mitigation that does not rely on the model's cooperation.
State what a privacy regulation requires of a stated data flow, without overstating legal certainty.

prerequisites.because: AI-specific threats sit on top of application security.
Guardrails are where safety requirements become enforceable behaviour.

supplemental_needed: OWASP LLM guidance and current regulatory summaries, dated, with the caveat that this area changes
source_coverage.notes: Awaiting sources. Lessons must not present legal advice; they state requirements as described by the cited sources and date them.

competencies.name: Cost and performance engineering
competencies.why: Inference and training cost is a product constraint, and measuring it is a distinct skill from optimising accuracy.
outcomes: Measure the cost per prediction of a stated system and identify the dominant term.
Explain the memory hierarchy's effect on inference speed and how batching changes it.
Propose a cost reduction and demonstrate it with a measurement rather than an estimate.

prerequisites.because: Cost is measured on the serving path.
Cost analysis is the accounting of numerical operations and their memory access.

supplemental_needed: Hardware and serving performance material with measurement practice
source_coverage.notes: Awaiting sources.

competencies.name: Responsible AI, fairness and documentation
competencies.why: A model that is accurate can still be harmful or unusable in a regulated context, and the obligations are increasingly explicit.
outcomes: Identify the stakeholders affected by a stated system and the harms that are plausible.
Measure a fairness property on a dataset and explain why the choice of metric is a value judgement.
Produce model documentation covering intended use, limitations and evaluation results.

prerequisites.because: Fairness measures are metrics with the same design questions.
Documentation is a lifecycle artifact.

supplemental_needed: Responsible-AI frameworks and model-card practice from reputable sources
source_coverage.notes: Not present in either roadmap as a named skill. Recorded as an audit addition with rationale; classified recommended rather than essential, and role-dependent in regulated sectors.

competencies.name: Technical writing and explanation
competencies.why: Technical work that cannot be explained to a colleague or an interviewer has limited effect.
outcomes: Write a document that lets a reader reproduce a stated result without contacting the author.
Explain a technical decision to a non-specialist audience without distortion.
Structure an explanation from problem to solution rather than chronologically.

supplemental_needed: Writing guidance from a reputable engineering organization
source_coverage.notes: Implicit in both roadmap sprints and the capstone; made explicit here so it can be assessed.

competencies.name: Code review and collaborative practice
competencies.why: Most professional code is written in a review loop, and the review is where design and correctness errors are caught cheaply.
outcomes: Review a change and separate blocking correctness issues from stylistic preferences.
Give feedback that states the problem rather than the preference.
Respond to review comments by reasoning about the change rather than complying automatically.

prerequisites.because: Reviews happen in the version-control workflow.
Design judgement is what most review comments are about.

supplemental_needed: Review practice guidance from a reputable engineering organization

competencies.name: Interview preparation and technical communication under constraint
competencies.why: Interviews test a specific, time-boxed variant of the same competencies and are gated by an ability to reason aloud.
outcomes: Solve a previously unseen algorithm problem while explaining the approach and its complexity.
Design a machine-learning system on a whiteboard covering data, serving, evaluation and failure.
Explain a project from one's own history and answer follow-up questions about its trade-offs.

prerequisites.because: Coding interviews assess algorithmic reasoning.
System-design interviews assess the design competency.
The performance is an explanation under time pressure.

supplemental_needed: Practice problem sets with known sources; interview questions must never be fabricated and attributed to a real employer
source_coverage.notes: Any question presented as having been asked in a real interview must name the verifiable source it came from; otherwise it is labelled as an original exercise.

competencies.name: Project work and portfolio construction
competencies.why: Employers screen on shipped work, and a project only demonstrates competence if its decisions are documented and its results are reproducible.
outcomes: Scope a project so that it can be completed and evaluated within a stated budget.
Deliver a project with reproducible setup, tests and a written design rationale.
Evaluate one's own project honestly against its original objective.

prerequisites.because: A portfolio project is expected to be tested.
A project that cannot be run by someone else demonstrates little.

supplemental_needed: None; the projects are authored, with rubrics
source_coverage.notes: The roadmap contains two project sprints and a final capstone, so project work exists in the plan but has no assessment criteria yet. This competency supplies them.

competencies.name: Reading technical material and research literacy
competencies.why: The field moves faster than any curriculum; the durable skill is the ability to extract and evaluate new material.
outcomes: Read a technical paper and state its claim, its method, its evidence and its limitations.
Distinguish a result that has been replicated from one that has only been published once.
Decide whether a claim requires re-checking given its date and version, and record when it was checked.

prerequisites.because: Extracting a claim requires reading for structure.

supplemental_needed: Guidance on reading research papers critically and on versioning fast-moving technical claims
source_coverage.notes: Section 1.2 of the supplied book discusses how to read the book and the role of exercises, which is directly on this competency at an introductory level.
